mechanism_name: Kernel-level read-only remount / immutable file attribute reasserted at boot
how_it_works:
This item bundles three distinct 'boring' (non-OEM) mechanisms that could each produce an apparent revert, evaluated separately because they predict different evidence:

(1) Standard fs_mgr read-only remount of /system during normal boot. On this device (system-as-root, two-stage init, no init.rc in the boot ramdisk), first-stage init mounts the system image per the compiled-in fstab and then switch_root's onto it, after which second-stage /system/bin/init reads init.rc from that same mounted filesystem and continues boot. fs_mgr commonly mounts /system read-only very early, before third-party processes can write to it. Critically, a read-only remount only blocks *future writes* through that mount point -- it does not rewrite or roll back bytes already committed to disk. If the edited init.rc bytes were genuinely present on the block device that first-stage init mounts, going read-only afterward would not un-edit them; init would simply read the already-edited content. A literal 'ro remount reverted my edit' story is therefore not mechanistically coherent by itself.

(2) ext4 immutable inode attribute (chattr +i / FS_IMMUTABLE_FL). If set, any write/rename/unlink to the file fails immediately with EPERM. There is no AOSP or stock kernel mechanism that silently re-applies +i to a specific file at boot; the flag is inode metadata that persists until explicitly cleared with chattr -i. This would produce write *failures*, not a silent content revert of a write that reportedly succeeded.

(3) Stale block cache / unsynced writes from the manual losetup workflow, OR (the variant explicitly invited by the task's parenthetical) the manual losetup offset/size not actually corresponding to the real boot-time mapping of the 'system' logical partition inside the dynamic 'super' container. Dynamic-partition logical partitions are not guaranteed to be a single contiguous extent -- liblp/lpmake can and does split a logical partition across multiple non-contiguous extents inside super (AOSP's dynamic-partitions documentation gives a concrete real-device example of system_a being split into two extents at different sector ranges). A manual 'losetup -o 1048576 --sizelimit 800915456 super_dev' captures only a single, first extent by construction. If (a) the real 'system' logical partition here is actually multi-extent and the edited inode's data blocks live in a later extent not covered by that single losetup mapping, or (b) the offset/size pair was derived against the wrong metadata slot (super's liblp header reports metadata_slot_count=2, unusual to see on a device otherwise described as non-A/B, raising the possibility that the by-name/lpdump output used for the offset calc came from a different slot than the one first-stage init actually loads at real boot), then the recovery-session edits are being written to and read back from a self-consistent but boot-irrelevant region of super. Every read/verify done through that same manual loop mapping would show the edit intact, while the real boot-time reconstruction (normally via device-mapper dm-linear built from the complete, correct extent list of the correct slot) uses a different underlying region that was never touched -- producing an apparently perfect 'revert' with zero exotic OEM logic involved.
fits_observed_symptoms:
(1) Write succeeds and is confirmed present pre-reboot -- consistent with all three sub-mechanisms: ro-remount hasn't happened yet in recovery, no evidence chattr +i was ever set, and a self-consistent-but-wrong loop mapping would also read back the edit fine.
(2) Survives unmount/remount within the same recovery session -- the most discriminating symptom. It FALSIFIES the 'stale/unflushed page cache' half of sub-mechanism (3): a clean umount forces writeback of dirty pages before completing, so if the edit persisted across an explicit unmount+remount, the bytes genuinely reached whatever block region the loop device pointed at. It does NOT falsify the extent/slot-mismatch half of (3), because that region could still be consistently wrong (always the same wrong place) across an unmount/remount that reuses the same losetup mapping.
(3) Reverts only after a real power-cycle boot -- fits the extent/slot-mismatch variant of (3) perfectly: only a real boot invokes the authoritative first-stage init / device-mapper reconstruction of the full, correct-slot extent list, the only path that would read a genuinely different region than the recovery-session loop mapping. Does not fit sub-mechanism (1) (ro-remount doesn't erase existing content) or (2) (immutable attribute blocks writes outright rather than silently reverting content after a successful write).
(4) boot_completed marker to /cache also never appears -- falls out for free under the extent/slot-mismatch theory: if init.rc itself never really changed on the copy that boots, the added boot_completed trigger was never present at boot either, so no marker gets written; not an independent puzzle. /cache is typically a separate by-name partition outside super's dynamic-partition pool, so this is explained through init.rc's absence, not any /cache-specific issue.
(5) AVB/vbmeta already disabled -- orthogonal; removes a competing explanation but doesn't confirm or deny these sub-mechanisms.
(6) /system is ext4, not squashfs -- necessary precondition for chattr/immutable-attribute and for read-write loop-mount editing to be meaningful at all; doesn't itself favor or disfavor any sub-mechanism given the timeline.
(7) Non-A/B, but super metadata_slot_count=2 -- the strongest circumstantial evidence for the slot-mismatch flavor of sub-mechanism (3): a metadata_slot_count of 2 on a device with no exposed by-name slot suffixes is exactly the kind of detail that would let an offset be computed from the wrong slot's metadata table with no obvious symptom until real boot uses the correct/active slot.
Overall: sub-mechanisms (1) 'pure ro-remount' and (2) 'immutable attribute reasserted' are logically incompatible with a write-that-succeeds-then-silently-reverts timeline and should be treated as effectively ruled out as literal explanations. The multi-extent / wrong-metadata-slot variant of (3) is not ruled out by any current evidence and is fully non-exotic (pure liblp/dynamic-partitions mechanics), making it the strongest remaining 'boring' hypothesis.
known_precedent: AOSP's dynamic-partitions documentation for device implementers explicitly documents that a single logical partition can be split across multiple, non-contiguous extents inside the super partition, with a concrete example of a real device's system_a partition fragmented into two extents at different sector ranges within super. This is documented, expected liblp/lpmake behavior, not a bug or OEM customization -- any tool (including a manual losetup calculation) that assumes a single contiguous region for a logical partition can silently operate on an incomplete or wrong slice of that partition's real data. AOSP's init/README and system-as-root/two-stage-init documentation confirm the general boot flow assumed here: first-stage init mounts system per the compiled fstab, switch_root's onto it, and second-stage init then reads init.rc from that same mounted filesystem -- no independent AOSP-standard step rewrites init.rc's content back to a prior version after a successful on-disk edit. No RK3326/Android-Go-STB/TXCZ-specific case of a stock fs_mgr ro-remount or chattr-based content revert was found; the closest indirectly relevant precedent is generic reports of ext4 read-write remounts unexpectedly failing back to read-only on certain Android kernels, which describes a remount *failure*, not a content-reversion mechanism, and is a materially different symptom.
likelihood: Low for the mechanism as literally named (fs_mgr read-only remount or a reasserted ext4 immutable attribute causing content reversion) -- neither can roll back already-committed bytes or explain a write that succeeds and is later silently undone. Medium for the closely related, equally non-exotic multi-extent/metadata-slot-mismatch variant of the manual losetup workflow, which fits every observed symptom and should be tested before crediting any bespoke OEM revert mechanism.
test_procedure:
All commands run from the existing Android Recovery root shell (adb root already confirmed working). Re-derive offsets independently rather than trusting the original calculation.

1. Dump super's actual metadata: `adb shell lpdump /dev/block/by-name/super`. Inspect the 'system' partition entry for ALL extents (start sector, length) and note which metadata slot (0 or 1) the listing came from. Also run `lpdump --slot 0 ...` and `lpdump --slot 1 ...` and diff the 'system' extent list between slots, given metadata_slot_count=2 on a device with no exposed by-name slot suffixes.
2. Compare the previously used losetup mapping (offset=1048576, size=800915456) against lpdump's authoritative extent list for the active slot. More than one extent, or a differing offset for the active slot, is likely sufficient by itself to confirm the hypothesis.
3. Reconstruct the real boot-time mapping with device-mapper (the same primitive fs_mgr uses), concatenating every extent lpdump reported for the correct slot: `adb shell dmsetup create system_diag --table "0 <len0> linear /dev/block/by-name/super <start0>\n<len0> <len1> linear /dev/block/by-name/super <start1>"` (one table line per extent), then `adb shell mount -o ro /dev/mapper/system_diag /mnt/system_real`.
4. Compare the reconstructed real mount's init.rc against the one previously edited via the naive losetup mount: `adb shell cmp /mnt/system_real/init.rc /path/to/previously/edited/init.rc`. A difference (reconstructed shows original, loop mount shows the edit) directly confirms the extent/slot-mismatch hypothesis.
5. Verify raw on-disk bytes at the byte offset where the edited text should appear, reading straight off the super block device with no filesystem/loop layer, for both the originally-assumed offset and the lpdump-derived correct offset: `adb shell dd if=/dev/block/by-name/super bs=1 skip=<byte_offset> count=200 2>/dev/null | hexdump -C`.
6. Rule out the immutable-attribute sub-mechanism (cheap, do regardless): `adb shell lsattr /mnt/system_real/init.rc` and on its parent directory, checking for an 'i' or 'a' flag; also re-check immediately after a fresh edit through the loop mount.
7. Rule out the unsynced-write sub-mechanism (cheap): before any future unmount, run `adb shell sync` and `adb shell blockdev --flushbufs /dev/loopX`, then repeat step 5's raw dd read to confirm bytes are physically present independent of mount/cache state.
8. Clean up: `adb shell umount /mnt/system_real; adb shell dmsetup remove system_diag`.
bypass_or_fix: If steps 4/5 confirm the extent/slot mismatch: stop computing losetup offsets by hand. Preferred fix: check whether recovery's first-stage init already exposes a correct device-mapper node for logical partitions (`adb shell ls -la /dev/block/mapper/`); if a 'system' (or 'system_a') node exists there, mount and edit THAT node directly instead of any manual losetup construction, since it reuses the same code path real boot uses. If no such node exists, always build the diagnostic dm-linear device from the complete, correct-slot extent list via `dmsetup create` (test_procedure step 3) and mount/edit through that node rather than a single-extent losetup guess; re-verify after any power cycle. After switching to the correct mapping, redo the init.rc edit and boot_completed-marker addition, power-cycle, and check /cache for the marker as the ultimate persistence test -- if it now survives, this hypothesis is confirmed and no OEM-level revert mechanism needs further investigation for this symptom. If immutable attribute is found instead: `chattr -i` before editing; if it recurs with nothing else running, that argues AGAINST 'boring' and should be escalated to the OEM-mechanism hypotheses. If unsynced writes are found: always `sync` and `blockdev --flushbufs` before every unmount going forward.
risk_level: Low / read-only diagnostic for lpdump, cmp, lsattr, dd reads, sync/flushbufs (non-destructive, don't touch the partitions being diagnosed). The dmsetup create + mount -o ro step is safe as long as a distinct diagnostic device-mapper name is used (e.g. 'system_diag') so it cannot collide with any production dm node, and it is removed afterward; mounting read-only prevents corruption even if the mapping is wrong. The bypass/fix carries the same risk as the already-validated manual editing workflow, plus the safety benefit of targeting the verified-correct region -- keep a backup copy of the original init.rc bytes before any further edit.
